subtitle: A map of the IETF's network management standards: which protocol fits which job, and what data model comes with it.

tldr.problem: There is no single IETF network management protocol. SNMP, syslog, IPFIX, NETCONF and a dozen others each do a different job, so a reader has to know which one to use and what comes with it.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC surveys the core protocols, describes their architecture and security models, groups the data models by layer and by management task, and adds an appendix that sorts the protocols by maturity, by push or pull, and by passive or active monitoring.
tldr.outcome: It is an Informational overview with no security implications of its own, written for working groups choosing a protocol and for implementers who need a map of the field.

facts.label: IPFIX mandatory transport

today: RFC 6632 is an Informational document, and the metadata shows no obsoleting and no updating RFC. It is an overview of the standards as they stood in 2012, so the maturity levels it records are the ones at the time of writing, and it points readers to the RFC Editor's search tool for current document status.

sections.title: Scope and Target Audience
sections.content:
This document gives an overview of the IETF network management standards and summarizes existing and ongoing development of IETF Standards Track network management protocols and data models. It refers to other overview documents where they exist and classifies the standards for easy orientation.

The audience is stated two ways. On one hand, IETF working groups, which aim to select appropriate standard management protocols and data models to address their needs. On the other hand, non-IETF Standards Development Organizations planning to use IETF management technologies and data models for the realization of management applications. The document can also be used to initiate a discussion between such bodies with the goal of gathering new requirements and detecting possible gaps, and it is directed at all interested parties, such as network administrators or newcomers to the IETF.

Section 2 gives an overview of the core network management standards, with a special focus on SNMP, syslog, IPFIX/PSAMP and NETCONF. Section 3 discusses protocols with a specific focus, such as IP address management or IP performance management. Section 4 discusses data models, such as MIB modules, IPFIX Information Elements, Syslog Structured Data Elements and YANG modules, and provides two complementary overviews of the data models standardized within the IETF: one broader, classifying models into generic infrastructure models and models matched to different layers, and one that structures them by the management application view, mapping them to the tasks fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security management.

Appendix A guides the reader for the high-level selection of management standards, classifying the protocols by criteria such as push versus pull mechanisms and passive versus active monitoring, and categorizing them by the management task they address and their data model extensibility. It can be used as a dispatcher to the corresponding chapter. Appendix B gives an overview of new work on Energy Management in the IETF.

The document mainly refers to Proposed, Draft or Internet Standard documents from the IETF, and references Best Current Practice documents where they are valuable. It does not cover OAM technologies on the data path, including MPLS forwarding plane and control plane protocols such as OAM of tunnels, MPLS-TP OAM and pseudowire, nor the corresponding management models and MIB modules. It also notes that the IETF had not developed specific technologies for the management of sensor networks, though IP-based sensors or constrained devices with very limited memory and CPU can use application-layer protocols for simple resource management and monitoring.

sections.title: SNMP: The Core Management Protocol
sections.content:
The SNMPv3 Framework builds upon both the original SNMPv1 and SNMPv2 Frameworks. The basic structure and components did not change between its versions, and comprise managed nodes, each with an SNMP entity providing remote access to management instrumentation, which is the agent; at least one SNMP entity with management applications, which is the manager; and a management protocol used to convey management information between the SNMP entities and that information.

The framework is modular, consisting of a generic protocol definition independent of the data it is carrying, a protocol-independent data definition language, an information repository containing the data set of management information definitions, the Management Information Base or MIB, and security and administration. The standards that build up the basis of the current framework are the SNMPv3 protocol, the modeling language SMIv2, and the MIB modules for different management issues.

SNMP is based on three conceptual entities: the Manager, the Agent and the MIB. In any configuration, at least one manager node runs SNMP management software. Typically, network devices such as bridges, routers and servers are equipped with an agent, which is responsible for providing access to a local MIB of objects that reflects the resources and activity at its node. Following the manager-agent paradigm, an agent can generate notifications and send them as unsolicited messages to the management application. SNMPv2 enhanced this with an Inform PDU, a bulk transfer capability and extensions such as an administrative model for access control, security extensions and Manager-to-Manager communication, and SNMPv2 entities can have a dual role as manager and agent. However, neither SNMPv1 nor SNMPv2 offers sufficient security features, so SNMPv3 has been issued. SNMPv1 has been declared Historic and its use is not recommended due to its lack of security features, and Introduction to Community-based SNMPv2 is an Experimental RFC that has also been declared Historic. Use of SNMPv3 is recommended, because of its security features, including support for authentication, encryption, message timeliness and integrity checking, and fine-grained data access controls.

SNMP is widely used for the monitoring of fault and performance data, and with its stateless nature it also works well for status polling and determining the operational state of specific functionality. The widespread use of counters in standard MIB modules permits interoperable comparison of statistics across devices from different vendors, which has been especially useful in monitoring bytes and packets going in and out over protocol interfaces. SNMP is often used to poll a basic parameter of a device, such as sysUpTime, to check operational liveliness and to detect discontinuities in counters. Some operators also use SNMP for configuration management in their environment.

Two parts make up the security model. The User-Based Security Model provides authentication and privacy services for SNMP, designed to secure against the primary threats of modification of information by an unauthorized entity and masquerade, and the secondary threats of message stream modification and disclosure. It does not secure against Denial of Service or attacks based on Traffic Analysis. It provides data integrity, data origin authentication, data confidentiality, and message timeliness with limited replay protection. The View-Based Access Control Model enables the configuration of agents to provide different levels of access to the agent's MIB, for example restricting some principals to view only performance-related statistics, or allowing only a single designated principal to update configuration parameters. It defines five elements that make up the access control model: groups, security level, contexts, MIB views and access policy.

One operational difficulty is noted. The User-Based Security Model was designed to be independent of other existing security infrastructures, so that it could function when third-party authentication services were not available, and as a result it uses a separate user and key-management infrastructure. Operators have reported that deploying a separate user and key-management infrastructure in order to use SNMPv3 is costly and hinders deployment. The SNMP Transport Subsystem extends the original SNMP architecture to enable the use of transport protocols to provide message security, unifying the administrative security management for SNMP and other management interfaces.
sections.plainLanguage: SNMP has three moving parts: the manager, the agent on each device, and the MIB, which is the tree of values the agent exposes. The manager pulls values and the agent pushes notifications. The first two versions had no security worth using, so version 3 added authentication, encryption and per-principal access control, at the cost of a separate key management system.

sections.title: Syslog, IPFIX and PSAMP
sections.content:
Syslog is a mechanism for distribution of logging information initially used on Unix systems. The IETF Syslog Protocol introduces a layered architecture allowing the use of any number of transport protocols, including reliable and secure transports, for transmission of syslog messages. It enables a machine to send system log messages across networks to event message collectors, and is simply designed to transport and distribute these event messages. By default no acknowledgements of the receipt are made, except where the reliable delivery extensions are used, and the protocol and process do not require stringent coordination between the transport sender and the receiver: transmission of syslog messages may be started on a device without a receiver being configured, or even physically present.

BSD syslog had little uniformity for the message format and the content of syslog messages, and the body of a BSD syslog message has traditionally been unstructured text, which is human friendly but difficult for applications to parse. The IETF Syslog Protocol standardized a new message header format, including timestamp, hostname, application and message ID, to improve filtering, interoperability and correlation between compliant implementations. It also introduces a mechanism for defining Structured Data Elements, which allow vendors to define their own structured data elements to supplement the standardized ones. Signed Syslog Messages defines a mechanism to add origin authentication, message integrity, replay resistance, message sequencing and detection of missing messages to transmitted syslog messages. For interoperability purposes, and especially in managed networks where the network path has been explicitly provisioned for UDP syslog traffic, syslog can be used over UDP, but the same document strongly recommends TLS to support congestion control and reliability. A TLS Transport Mapping and a DTLS Transport Mapping are also defined.

IPFIX defines a push-based data export mechanism for transferring IP flow information in a compact binary format from an Exporter to a Collector. The IPFIX Architecture defines the components involved: a Metering Process generating Flow Records, an Exporting Process that sends metered flow information using the IPFIX protocol, and a Collecting Process that receives flow information as IPFIX Data Records. The IPFIX Protocol specifies SCTP as the mandatory transport protocol to implement, with TCP and UDP as optional alternatives, and SCTP is used with its Partial Reliability extension. IPFIX transmits IP flow information in Data Records containing Information Elements whose unit and semantics are defined by the IPFIX Information Model; only their values need to be carried on the wire, which allows efficient transport of large numbers of measured flow values. The Information Model is extensible, with new Information Elements registered at IANA, and IPFIX also supports proprietary, enterprise-specific ones. The PSAMP protocol extends IPFIX by transferring information on individual packets, with a set of sampling and filtering techniques for packet selection.

Two practical points follow. The Metering and Exporting Processes are configured out of band, because the IPFIX protocol is a push mechanism only and cannot configure the Exporter; the actual configuration of selection processes, caches, Exporting Processes and Collecting Processes is executed using the NETCONF protocol. And the IPFIX and PSAMP protocols define no new security mechanisms, relying instead on the security mechanism of the underlying transport protocol, such as TLS and DTLS, while privacy, integrity and authentication of the Exporter and Collector are important security requirements.
sections.plainLanguage: Syslog carries log messages from devices to collectors, and the message format was standardised so that log collectors can parse it. IPFIX carries flow records: the exporter measures traffic and pushes a compact set of values to a collector. PSAMP does the same for individual sampled packets.

sections.title: NETCONF and YANG
sections.content:
The IAB workshop on Network Management determined a list of advanced requirements for configuration management: robustness, meaning minimizing disruptions and maximizing stability; a task-oriented view; extensibility for new operations; standardized error handling; a clear distinction between configuration data and operational state; distribution of configurations to devices under transactional constraints; single- and multi-system transactions and scalability in the number of transactions and managed devices; operations on selected subsets of management data; dumping and reloading a device configuration in a textual format in a standard manner across multiple vendors and device types; a human interface and a programmatic interface; a data modeling language with a human-friendly syntax; easy conflict detection and configuration validation; and secure transport, authentication and robust access control.

The NETCONF protocol provides mechanisms to install, manipulate and delete the configuration of network devices and aims to address those requirements. It uses an XML-based data encoding for the configuration data as well as the protocol messages, and the protocol operations are realized on top of a simple and reliable Remote Procedure Call layer. A key aspect of NETCONF is that it allows the functionality of the management protocol to closely mirror the native command-line interface of the device. Optional capabilities include Event Notifications, providing an asynchronous message notification delivery service, and Partial Locking, which introduces fine-grained locking of the configuration datastore to enable transactions on parts of it. A data model for monitoring the protocol itself covers datastores, sessions, locks and statistics.

NETCONF connections are required to provide authentication, data integrity, confidentiality and replay protection, and the protocol depends on the underlying transport for this capability, for example TLS or SSH. The SSH transport protocol is the mandatory transport binding, with TLS, BEEP over TLS and SOAP over HTTP over TLS as optional bindings. The NETCONF Access Control Model provides standard mechanisms to restrict protocol access to particular users with a pre-configured subset of operations and content.

YANG is the data modeling language that defines the semantics of operational and configuration data, notifications and operations. It maps directly to XML-encoded content on the wire and serves as the normative description of NETCONF data models. YANG provides the means to define hierarchical data models, and supports reusable data types and groupings that can be reused across module boundaries. It supports the distinction between configuration and state data, and supports modeling event notifications and the specification of operations that extend the base NETCONF operations. It allows the expression of constraints by means of type restrictions and XPath 1.0 expressions, which can also be used to make certain portions of a data model conditional. Its augmentation mechanism allows the seamless augmentation of standard data models with proprietary extensions. Data models can be partitioned into collections of features, allowing low-end devices to implement only the core features while high-end devices may support all of them, with the supported features announced through the NETCONF capability exchange. The syntax is compact and optimized for human readers, and devices implementing standard data models can document deviations from the data model in separate YANG modules.
sections.plainLanguage: NETCONF is for configuration: it reads and writes device configuration in XML, over SSH, and it separates what you configured from what the device is actually doing. YANG is the language that describes what the configuration may contain, so that a client and a device agree on the shape of the data.

sections.title: The Data Models and How to Choose One
sections.content:
The data models defined by the IETF fall into categories. Generic infrastructure data models provide core abstractions that many other data models are built upon: the interfaces data model in the IF-MIB provides the basic notion of network interfaces and allows expressing stacking and layering relationships between interfaces, and also provides basic monitoring objects widely used for performance and fault management; the Entity MIB exports the containment hierarchy of the physical entities, slots, modules and ports, that make up a networking device, and is a key data model for inventory management, with Entity State MIB modelling the states and alarms of those entities.

Then come the models matched to the layers of the Internet. Link-layer models cover the link layers IP runs over, such as ADSL, VDSL, GMPLS, ISDN, ATM, cable modems and Ethernet, and typically extend the generic network interfaces data model with interface-type specific information, with most focused on monitoring for performance and fault management. Network-layer models cover IP and ICMP and their extensions, the popular unicast routing protocols OSPF, IS-IS and BGP-4, the multicast routing protocol PIM, and the detailed models for performance measurements in the form of IP Performance Metrics. Transport-layer models cover TCP, UDP and SCTP. Application-layer models exist for specific application protocols such as SIP, and generic application MIB modules have been less successful in gaining widespread deployment. Finally, network management infrastructure data models concern the management system itself: MIB modules for monitoring and configuring SNMP, generic functions for calculating expressions over MIB objects, thresholding and event generation, event notification logging, models to represent alarms, models that allow the execution of basic reachability and path discovery tests, and the RMON family of MIB modules providing remote monitoring functions from the data link layer up to the application layer.

The second view matches the models to the management tasks, the FCAPS view of fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security management. Some models span several categories by design, and the technology-specific models, such as transmission and protocol MIBs, are not listed there. Appendix A gives further ways to narrow the choice. The first classifies the protocols by their standard maturity in the IETF, from Internet Standard through Proposed and Draft Standard to Informational. The second matches protocols to management tasks. The third separates push from pull: a pull mechanism is characterized by the network management system pulling the management information out of network elements when needed, and a push mechanism by the network elements pushing it, either when the information is available or on a regular basis. The fourth separates passive monitoring, which performs network traffic monitoring, device monitoring or accounting of resource consumption, from active monitoring, which relies on the injection of specific traffic, called synthetic traffic, which is then monitored.
sections.plainLanguage: The data models come in two arrangements: one by layer, so that link-layer, network-layer and transport-layer models sit alongside generic ones such as interfaces and physical entities; and one by job, so that fault, configuration, accounting, performance and security management each have their own set. The appendix then sorts the protocols by how far they have progressed and by whether the manager fetches data or the device pushes it.

sections.title: Security Considerations
sections.content:
This document gives an overview of IETF network management standards and summarizes existing and ongoing development of IETF Standards Track network management protocols and data models. As such, it does not have any security implications in or of itself. For each specific technology discussed in the document, a summary of its security usage has been given in the corresponding chapters, and in a few cases, such as for SNMP, a detailed description of the developed security mechanisms has been provided.

The reader's attention is drawn in particular to the security discussions in the sections on the SNMP security and access control models, the User-Based Security Model, the View-Based Access Control Model and the SNMP Transport Security Model; secure syslog message delivery; the use of secure NETCONF message transport and the NETCONF Access Control Model; message authentication for DHCP; security for RADIUS in conjunction with EAP and IEEE 802.1X authenticators; the built-in and transport security for the Diameter Base Protocol; transport security for CAPWAP; the built-in security for ANCP; security for ACAP and XCAP; and the data models for security management. The authors also refer readers to the detailed security consideration sections of the specific management standards described in this document, which contain comprehensive discussion of the security implications of each protocol and mechanism.
sections.plainLanguage: The overview itself carries no security risk. It points instead at the security sections of each standard, and lists the ones worth reading before implementing a protocol.

items.title: Hierarchical models
items.text: Data models are hierarchical, with reusable data types and groupings that can cross module boundaries.

items.title: Configuration versus state
items.text: The two are modelled separately, and notifications and extra operations can be modelled too.

items.title: Constraints
items.text: Type restrictions and XPath 1.0 expressions can constrain a model and make parts of it conditional.

items.title: Augmentation
items.text: Standard models can be extended seamlessly with proprietary extensions.

items.title: Features
items.text: A model can be split into features, so small devices implement only the core and announce what they support.

items.title: Deviations
items.text: A device can document where it departs from a standard model in a separate module.
